reviews.text: You stand up from the poker table where you've spent the last month playing Balatro. Dazed, you wander over to another corner of the casino, where you see a new roulette table being set up. "Bingle Bingle?" you wonder to yourself, "Odd name for a roulette game, but let's give it a shot." Congratulations, you have just lost another month to a casino roguelike.

The difference between Poker and Roulette is that Poker is fun. Predictably, this is also the difference between Bingle Bingle and Balatro. I feel bad trashing this game because it's pretty obvious the developer put a lot of thought and effort into spinning-off Balatro without directly copying it. Unfortunately it just doesn't work, for some reasons that are obvious and for some I can't quite place my finger on. The biggest problem is complexity; while Balatro is easy to grasp and difficult to master, Bingle Bingle is the opposite. Descriptions of the game's many mechanics and upgrades are overly lengthy; they lack elegant wording or usage and feature far too many finicky calculations and percentages, the consequences of which are not easily understood. Within 5 minutes and before I had even left the tutorial my mind was spinning from all the game was throwing at me, and I had lost basically all enthusiasm. I only kept playing out of respect for the premise. Unfortunately, things did not improve. Another huge flaw is the UI, possibly the most important aspect of a technical rogue-like after gameplay. There are just too many elements on the screen at a time, many with unclear meanings or icons that get swept up in the chaos. A lot of elements lack hover-over info boxes, which led me to just ignore them rather than try to develop an understanding. When they did have info-boxes, the information was often very poorly conveyed with too many keywords and interactions, which similarly is rooted in the game's complexity creep. These points lead to the game's biggest flaw, the one that truly makes it not fun (besides being based on a machine that glorifies coin flips): it's shallow. I beat the game on my second run, the first being the tutorial, through no strategy other than clicking on the shiniest items in the shop and rolling ball after ball with a single bet on black tiles. There is no reward for trying to understand all the complexity, for trying to craft a strategy out of the immense amount of information thrown at you. At the end of the day all it takes to win is a pattern-seeking brain and a functioning mouse. I don't feel that this is intentional on the developer's part, and it saddens me. At this point I just hope someone makes a quality rogue-like version of Blackjack; Resident Evil 7 showed that the potential of adapting that game is far greater than that of roulette.

I love the concept and aesthetic of this game, but i doubt this dev will be able to deliver an actually good game any time soon.

I find the trend of Balatro-likes fascinating. Watching the flood of them and the way each takes the fundamental core of Balatro—a simple, familiar game with the mechanics of a deckbuilder slammed on top—then develops it is interesting. I am watching the formation of an entirely new subgenre in real time, and with it, the narrowing of the rules of what qualifies and then pushes at the limits of those rules. Some games do this successfully. Some games understand the heart of what makes a Balatro-like work, and when they do, they create something new and excellent. Other games are Bingle Bingle. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3679380916 Bingle Bingle is a roulette-based Balatro-like. As with any Balatro-like, players move through a series of escalating minimum scores, punctuated by shops and boss rounds, and ending if the player is unable to meet the minimum score. Players take the relatively familiar rules of roulette and turn them on their head by modifying the roulette wheel, the ball, and everything else that could possibly be modified. On the surface, there’s nothing wrong with the premise of Bingle Bingle. Balatro-likes are at their best when they start with a simple and understandable base, and, in theory, there is nothing simpler than roulette. Wheel spin, ball land, house wins. What I learned playing Bingle Bingle, though, is that this is not how roulette works, or is at least, not the entirety of how roulette works. There are a range of betting strategies—do you bet on a colour? A type of number? A block of numbers? A line?—that, for anyone unfamiliar with roulette seem arcane at best. I learned a lot about roulette from Bingle Bingle, perhaps more than the devs would have wanted me to. I learned about pockets, tokens, balls, and of course, the range of bets, all of which, again, should be simple and straightforward, until I went to modify it. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3679381179 I would argue that the soul of any Balatro-like is in the satisfaction of warping a game’s rules to the point of unrecognisability. When I’m playing Balatro, I consider it a victory when my deck is nothing but twenty-three aces of diamonds, each giving me a ridiculously disgusting modifier. The rules and reality of poker lie in the dust, crushed beneath my determination to twist this deck into something that works for me and me alone. Bingle Bingle does this as well. I can, if I so choose, turn the entire board into a red 2, repeating endlessly as the ball buffets between them, indecisive about which specific two is speaking to it. I can modify each token to generate a big ball, or many balls, or a ball that is not a ball. There are many ways I can shape this roulette wheel, and the game is happy to throw as many of them at me as it can. But it’s in that desire to give me many options that Bingle Bingle begins to miss the point. What makes a Balatro-like work is that its simplicity is deceptive. Behind the simple rules and the familiar game lies a vast variety of ways to break those rules and destroy that game. Bingle Bingle at no point pretends to be simple. From the outset, it introduces a bivvy of undefined terms and icons, some of which I still don’t understand after four hours of play. It presents a huge world of options, missing that, where a Balatro-like succeeds is not in recreating the immense complexity of a traditional deckbuilder, but in masking that complexity behind a limited set of easily understood mechanics. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3679381358 Learning to navigate complexity is, of course, a fundamental part of a deckbuilder, though I would argue that, despite having the word “deck” in it, Bingle Bingle is not a deckbuilder. However, there comes a point where the sheer amount of complexity comes full circle again, where there is no longer a sense of building something that will control the randomness, but rather, that the number of options are beyond controlling. Attempting to build towards anything in particular becomes an exercise in futility. Crafting what you have into something coherent becomes impossible. The game itself has too many moving parts to truly be controlled, and instead, just feels random and unsatisfying. Even in the runs where I win, the lack of labelling and the sheer amount of stuff happening makes it difficult to understand why I’ve won. The techniques and tactics I’ve learned from dozens of other deckbuilders don’t work here because there is too much going on to control. I can perfect my tokens, but in doing so, I lose the wheel. I can focus on the wheel, but then the badges slip away. There is too much to be able to control in any meaningful sense, and too little time or resources in which to do it. The core of what makes a Balatro-like is gone. The simplicity masking an underlying complexity is gone. All there is too many mechanics to be satisfying, and too little explanation of what they are and why they matter for me to care. Once you finish a run of Bingle Bingle, the game offers an endless mode where you can see just how far your build will get. However, rather than following the same pattern of two normal wheels, then a boss with a modified ruleset, Bingle Bingle’s endless mode instead puts the player in an endless string of bosses, one modified ruleset after another. There is no way to plan for these bosses, no way to predict which one is next, just bosses that may or may not randomly destroy everything that was built so far with no way to work around it. This, in many ways, summarises my experience playing Bingle Bingle. I can understand the mechanics, and I can plan a build around the badges or quests or initial starting bonuses I draw. I can plan these things, but none of it will matter. There are too many mechanics for me to get the upgrades I need. The board will end up random, and there is nothing I can do to change it. So I throw the ball. I see where it lands. And I recapture the feeling of playing actual roulette. Yea, I dunno what it is, but the game just isn't as fun as I thought it'd be. It doesn't feel like there is any randomness to the game. The amount of times the wheel has landed on my number without anything attempting to encourage it to, is crazy in comparison to how Roulette normally plays out. Plus when you add the upgrades, and all the extras, the game is just a dull rinse repeat cycle that just doesn't work for some reason. I dunno if it's that there isn't enough turns/spins you can do(?) or what, but each round just feels far too short, then suddenly you are back at the shop. You will spend 90% of your time looking at the shop and upgrades window, and 10% of the time actually spinning the wheel and playing. It's just boring. It should be the other way around. They should have a higher amount of chips to achieve per round, and like 15 spins, not 5 on average. It simply feels like the wrong direction was chosen for gameplay. The game isn't "Bad," but it is just sort of boring and extremely repetitive. I'd rather be watching the ball spin around longer, with more actual randomness, then a guided experience the way the game is now. There is just too much in place to ensure the ball lands exactly where you want it to, which makes the idea of it being a roulette wheel irrelevant. PS: Things like the ice mechanic shouldn't exist, it's just dumb and further exasperates the above issues, drastically limiting where the ball can land. It's like the devs wanted to further shoot themselves in the foot after already doing so.

I probably got my monies worth, but I doubt I'll open the game again ever.

[h1]蛮有趣的随机游戏——《疯狂轮盘》[/h1] 先说结论，游戏像是一个轮盘版的小丑牌，玩家需要尽可能的利用各种手段，来完成既定目标任务。 有一定难度，但也充满乐趣！ 在《疯狂轮盘》中，游戏由36个球袋的大转盘构成，当球落入对应球袋后，即可获得相应分数。 每回合都有一个目标筹码，完成即可通关。 玩家每局拥有5个筹码。每个筹码有两种选择，一是选择就是类似红黑、或者是1-18，双数，甚至有单数、19-36之类的倍数。 只要你的小球投入选择中，猜中即可获得不同倍数的奖励。 二是小球，这回合你不进行倍数设定，直接进行投掷，到哪得到多少分数。 每次胜利后，都可以进行一次购买代币升级，比如红黑/连线等，升级点数可以提高中的概率。 同时，游戏内置商店，可以购买附带能力的球，这个超级实用。 类似于多重球，每次可以出来3个以上。 或者是大球，变得超级大！对应的球可以装在代币上！ 甚至还有球袋，就是将不同颜色的球袋变成你想要的。 还有一些额外加成，就是在这个点数上，获得额外倍数。 同时，每一局都有特殊能力，比如弓箭手，使用3次秋后，可以选择下一颗球的落点，是不超级牛逼！ 配合你提前下注好的代币，即可直接获得超多分数。 每当击败boss后，玩家可以选择强力效果，比如单色——所有下注变为彩色。 贪焰——提供一个额外的贪焰代币，使用十次后，额外获得加成。 一杆进洞——幸运+2,400%一杆进洞奖励。 这些加成怎么说呢，有一定用处，但不是核心！ 当你用完所有代币后，仍可利用仅有的3点生命值进行游戏，消耗完后，游戏随之结束。 整体体验下来，《疯狂轮盘》作为一款超带劲的 “轮盘构筑” 策略游戏，通过各种小球、筹码分配、代币、槽位和徽章玩转组合，来达到高额分数。 玩起来还算不错，但有一定上手难度，需要玩家仔细学习！ [quote]欢迎关注『 [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/45525570/] 桃你欢心 [/url]』 [b] 桃影扶风评百戏，落墨如歌写人间[/b][/quote]

Had a few fun hours with this game. Didn't look at the reviews before I played it and coming here to see it at mixed was a shock. The only thing I didn't like about the game was the small amount of content. The game took me about 10 hours to beat which feels a little bit under the sweet spot. Also I know I probably have a few unlocks I need to get but it felt like I was seeing a lot of the same badges again and again in the same run. Thats where the bad stuff ends though. The game flow is smooth, and the way all the upgrades work together allows for so many playstyles. My personal favourite was going for no bets and multiball. Something about spinning 10 or so balls at once was very satisfying. The mechanics fit together well, and are just difficult enough that it takes an hour or two to understand them. The boss characters have mechanics that make it tough but don't feel unfair, and everything overall feels balanced well. All of the odd/gimmicky playstyles have enough upgrades to support them to the point they don't feel like gimmicks which is something I see a lot of other deck builders do. All in all, could not reccomend this game more.
